reading.reading_name: Guidance for Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets

drills.los_text: demonstrate a thorough knowledge of the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct by interpreting the Code and Standards in various situations involving issues of professional integrity
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets

questions.stem: Barnes, president and controlling shareholder of SmartTown, accepts a tender offer for the company at nearly double its market price and mentions it to his sister, who tells her daughter, whose husband, Staple, passes it to his broker, Halsey; Halsey immediately buys SmartTown stock. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is most likely violated by:

options.A: both Staple and Halsey.
options.B: Halsey only.
options.C: neither Staple nor Halsey.

rationales.A: The information regarding the pending sale is both material and nonpublic: a tender offer at nearly double the market price would clearly affect the share price, and it has not been disseminated to the market. Staple violated Standard II(A) by communicating the inside information to his broker, and Halsey also violated the standard by buying the shares on the basis of material nonpublic information.
rationales.B: This reflects the misconception that only the person who executes a trade can be liable. Staple also violated Standard II(A): communicating material nonpublic information to his broker is itself prohibited use of that information, whether or not Staple traded on it himself.
rationales.C: Passing material nonpublic information along a chain of family members does not dilute or cleanse it. The information was still both material and nonpublic when it reached Halsey, so Staple's communication of it and Halsey's purchase on the basis of it each breached Standard II(A).

questions.stem: Peter is assisting with a secondary offering for Bright Ideas. On a video call in his office he learns that the company's earnings projections have dropped significantly, while salespeople and portfolio managers walk in and out and overhear him, and firm personnel trade the stock before the call ends. Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information is most likely violated by:

options.A: The salespeople and portfolio managers only.
options.B: Peter and the personnel who traded.
options.C: No one at the firm.

rationales.A: Peter is not in the clear. He violated Standard II(A) because he failed to prevent the transfer and misuse of material nonpublic information to others in his firm; that failure to contain the information is itself the violation, and the traders' misuse of it compounds his breach rather than replacing it.
rationales.B: Peter violated Standard II(A) because he failed to prevent the transfer and misuse of material nonpublic information to others in his firm. Peter's firm should have adopted information barriers to prevent the communication of nonpublic information between departments of the firm. Firm personnel who are members or candidates and who traded on the information also violated Standard II(A) by trading on inside information.
rationales.C: Not trading personally does not clear Peter. He violated Standard II(A) by failing to prevent the transfer and misuse of material nonpublic information within his firm, and the personnel who traded on the dropped earnings projections violated the standard as well.

questions.stem: Levenson, invited along with a company's ten largest shareholders to meet its finance director in Taipei, is told there that the workforce is expected to strike next Friday and cripple production. In deciding whether she may use this information to change her rating, Levenson most appropriately:

options.A: treats the information as immaterial.
options.B: determines whether the information is public.
options.C: treats the information as public.

rationales.A: A strike expected to cripple production is material, because it would likely affect the share price. Materiality is not what disposes of this case; whether the information has been made public is.
rationales.B: Levenson must first determine whether the material information is public. According to Standard II(A), if the company has not made this information public, she must not use it, and a small group forum does not qualify as a method of public dissemination. Because the finance director disclosed the expected strike at a private meeting with the ten largest shareholders, the information remains nonpublic, and Levenson cannot act on it until the company discloses it broadly.
rationales.C: A select small-group forum is not a method of public dissemination. Disclosing the expected strike to the ten largest shareholders left the information nonpublic, so Levenson may not rely on it to change her rating.

questions.stem: Fechtman is weighing whether to hold or sell her position in an oil and gas exploration company. Her doctor, who casually follows the markets, mentions his belief that the company will soon be bought by a multinational conglomerate. Under Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information, Fechtman most likely:

options.A: may trade only after asking the company to confirm or deny the rumor.
options.B: may trade on the basis of her own analysis.
options.C: may not trade on the information at all.

rationales.A: No confirmation step is required before Fechtman acts. The prohibition in Standard II(A) attaches only to information that is both material and nonpublic, and the casual, unreliable source here means the materiality threshold is never reached. Because the information is not material, there is nothing for the company to confirm or deny on Fechtman's behalf, and she is free to proceed on her own analysis of the hold-or-sell decision.
rationales.B: Although information on an expected takeover bid may be generally material and nonpublic, in this case the source of the information is unreliable, so the information cannot be considered material. Materiality turns on the substance of the information and on the reliability of its source: a vague secondhand belief voiced by a doctor who only casually follows the markets, with no connection to the company or to the transaction, does not meet the threshold. Therefore Fechtman is not prohibited from trading the stock based on this information, and she may act on her own analysis.
rationales.C: Takeover information is not automatically material nonpublic information. Here the source — a doctor casually following the markets — is unreliable, so the tip lacks the reliability needed for materiality, and no blanket prohibition on trading arises. Treating every rumor of an acquisition as off limits would bar members from acting on their own research whenever a market rumor happens to be circulating.

questions.stem: Teja, a buy-side analyst, studies SFC's financial reports, visits its operations, and talks with designers and retailers. He concludes that the company's extravagant new designs are not selling well and that next-quarter earnings will drop, and he issues a sell recommendation before SFC reports. Teja most likely:

options.A: violated Standard II(A) by publishing before the earnings release.
options.B: violated Standard II(A) by anticipating material earnings information.
options.C: did not violate Standard II(A).

rationales.A: A conclusion assembled from public information and nonmaterial nonpublic pieces may be acted on and published without waiting for the company's own release. Requiring Teja to hold his recommendation until SFC reports would strip research of its value, since the point of fundamental analysis is to reach the conclusion before the market does.
rationales.B: Anticipating an earnings outcome is not the same as possessing it. Teja's conclusion was assembled from public information and from pieces of nonmaterial nonpublic information, which is precisely what the mosaic theory permits; he did not obtain the company's quarterly earnings data itself.
rationales.C: While company information on quarterly earnings data is material and nonpublic, Teja based his conclusion about the earnings drop on public information and on pieces of nonmaterial nonpublic information, such as the opinions of designers and retailers. Under the mosaic theory, an analyst may combine public information with nonmaterial nonpublic information and act on the resulting judgment, even when that judgment concerns a figure the company has not yet released. Therefore, trading or issuing a recommendation based on Teja's correct conclusion is not prohibited by Standard II(A).

questions.stem: A senior automobile analyst speaks with company representatives, salespeople, labor leaders, regional currency analysts, and banking officials. He concludes that a new model will not meet expectations, that restructuring may face union opposition, that currency depreciation is pressuring margins, and that banks may take a tougher stance. He retains his support material and changes his rating on Turgot Chariots from outperform to underperform. Clement most likely:

options.A: violated Standard II(A) by using inside knowledge from company representatives.
options.B: violated Standard II(A) by relying on nonpublic conversations.
options.C: did not violate Standard II(A).

rationales.A: Nothing Clement obtained from the company's representatives was itself material. Each piece he gathered was either already public or, standing alone, immaterial, and assembling such pieces into a valuable investment conclusion is the mosaic theory at work rather than the use of inside knowledge.
rationales.B: A conversation being nonpublic does not make the information in it material. Nonpublic conversations are permissible sources when what they convey is nonmaterial, and the conclusion Clement built from them may be used; retaining his support material also lets him demonstrate the basis for the rating change.
rationales.C: To reach a conclusion about the value of the company, Clement pieced together a number of nonmaterial or public bits of information that affect Turgot Chariots — the reception of the new model, the likelihood of union opposition to restructuring, the margin pressure from depreciation of the Korean won, and the posture of the company's banks. No single item was material nonpublic information, and the insight lies in the synthesis. Therefore, under the mosaic theory, Clement did not violate Standard II(A) in drafting the report, and his retention of the supporting material documents that basis.

questions.stem: While preparing for a television interview, Clement mentions to the producers and to his acquaintance Zito the information he will discuss, including a change in his opinion on Turgot Chariots. Before the interview airs, Zito sells her Turgot holdings and telephones her father. Zito most likely:

options.A: did not violate Standard II(A), because she did not know Clement's reasoning.
options.B: did not violate Standard II(A), because only Clement disclosed the information.
options.C: violated Standard II(A), because advance notice of the opinion change is material.

rationales.A: Knowledge of the underlying analysis is not required. When Zito receives advance notice that a prominent analyst's opinion is changing, she knows that notice will have a material impact on the stock price even though she is unaware of Clement's underlying reasoning, and that is enough to make the information material and nonpublic in her hands.
rationales.B: Clement's disclosure created the exposure, but it does not absolve Zito. She is not a client of Clement; she simply obtained early access to material nonpublic information prior to its publication, and her trades were based on it. Her own conduct violates the standard independently of his.
rationales.C: When Zito receives advance notice of Clement's change of opinion, she knows it will have a material impact on the stock price, even if she is not aware of Clement's underlying reasoning. She is not a client of Clement but obtains early access to material nonpublic information prior to publication, so her trades are based on material nonpublic information and she violated Standard II(A). Zito further violated the standard by relaying the information to her father: it would not matter whether he or any other family member traded, because the act of providing the information is itself the violation.

questions.stem: Kellogg, a retired investment professional, owns shares of National Bank. His close friend Mayfield, a senior executive at the bank, tells him that National will surprise the investment community with excellent earnings. Believing that Mayfield would not break the law, Kellogg doubles his position, and the stock later falls 60% on combined news. Kellogg most likely:

options.A: did not violate Standard II(A), because he trusted Mayfield to obey the law.
options.B: violated Standard II(A) by purchasing additional shares.
options.C: did not violate Standard II(A), because he lost money on the purchase.

rationales.A: Kellogg's trust in his friend does not transfer responsibility for the trade. It is the member's or candidate's own responsibility to make sure, before executing investment actions, that comments about earnings are not material nonpublic information, and a senior executive's preview of an earnings surprise plainly is.
rationales.B: Even though Kellogg believes that Mayfield would not break the law by disclosing inside information, Kellogg violated Standard II(A) by purchasing additional shares of National. A senior executive's advance word that the bank will surprise the market with excellent earnings is material and nonpublic, and the fact that he lost money on the purchase does not absolve him for trading on it. It is the member's or candidate's responsibility to make sure, before executing investment actions, that comments about earnings are not material nonpublic information.
rationales.C: The outcome of the trade is irrelevant to the violation. Standard II(A) is breached when the investment action is taken on material nonpublic information, so losing money on the additional shares does not absolve Kellogg; profit or loss affects neither the materiality of Mayfield's comment nor Kellogg's duty to verify it beforehand.

questions.stem: Nadler, a trader, receives a text message from a trader at another firm whom he has known for years, saying he believes a software company will report strong earnings in two days. Nadler already holds an unrelated buy order in that stock from one of his portfolio managers and completes it aggressively before the earnings release. Nadler most likely:

options.A: violated Standard II(A) by trading ahead of the earnings release.
options.B: did not violate Standard II(A).
options.C: violated Standard II(A) by not confirming the rumor with the company.

rationales.A: Trading before an earnings release is a violation only when the trader holds material nonpublic information. An unsubstantiated whisper from a trader with no demonstrated business tie to the issuer is market noise, not material nonpublic information, so completing the portfolio manager's independent order was permissible.
rationales.B: There are often rumors and whisper numbers before a release of any kind, and the text message from the other trader would most likely be considered market noise. Unless Nadler knew that the trader had an ongoing business relationship with the public firm, he had no reason to suspect he was receiving material nonpublic information that would prevent him from completing the trading request of the portfolio manager. The buy order originated independently with the portfolio manager, and Nadler's duty of best execution supports completing it promptly.
rationales.C: No confirmation step is required. The text message is market noise rather than material nonpublic information, and the buy order Nadler is working came independently from the portfolio manager, so there is no rumor that he must take to the software company before acting.

questions.stem: McCoy is a senior drug analyst whose firm engages a service that connects her by telephone with experts in cancer treatment, which enhances her understanding of the latest therapies. She neither asks for nor receives preliminary trial results or similar confidential data. McCoy most likely:

options.A: violated Standard II(A) by consulting a paid expert network.
options.B: violated Standard II(A) by not disclosing the consulting arrangement.
options.C: did not violate Standard II(A).

rationales.A: Paid expert networks are not a prohibited source of information. A violation arises only if material nonpublic information is solicited or received through the arrangement, and McCoy is allowed to seek advice from professionals within the industry she follows.
rationales.B: No public disclosure of the consulting arrangement is required for McCoy to rely on what she learns. Because she obtained no material nonpublic information from the calls, there is nothing about the engagement that must be disseminated to the market before she uses the insight in her evaluation.
rationales.C: McCoy is appropriately using expert networks to enhance her evaluation process. She neither asked for nor received information that may be considered material and nonpublic, such as preliminary trial results, and McCoy is allowed to seek advice from professionals within the industry that she follows. The analyst's obligation is to judge, for each conversation, whether what she has been told reaches the materiality threshold; general education about therapies does not.

questions.stem: Watson, a hedge fund analyst, uses outside experts arranged through networks whose agreements contain policies deterring the transfer of material nonpublic information. On a call, a scientist leading tests of a new semiconductor product expresses disappointment with its performance. Watson relays this to others at the fund, who sell the existing position and buy put options. Watson most likely:

options.A: did not violate Standard II(A), because the network's agreements barred disclosure.
options.B: violated Standard II(A) by relaying the information to the fund.
options.C: did not violate Standard II(A), because only the consultant disclosed anything.

rationales.A: Watson cannot simply rely on the agreements signed by individuals who participate in expert networks that state that he has not received information that would prohibit his trading activity. He must make his own determination whether information he received through these arrangements reaches a materiality threshold that would influence his trading, and a test engineer's disappointment with an unreleased product's performance does.
rationales.B: Watson violated Standard II(A) by passing along material nonpublic information concerning the ongoing product tests, which the fund used to trade in the securities and options of the related company. Watson cannot simply rely on the agreements signed by individuals who participate in expert networks that state that he has not received information that would prohibit his trading activity; he must make his own determination whether information he received through these arrangements reaches a materiality threshold that would influence his trading. The fund's sale of the position and purchase of puts shows that the information was in fact material.
rationales.C: Responsibility does not stop with the source. Watson violated Standard II(A) by passing along material nonpublic information about the ongoing tests, which the fund then traded on in both the shares and the options; recipients of such information bear their own responsibility for how they use it and may not treat whatever a consultant volunteers as freely usable.

questions.stem: Andrews has heard rumors of a possible merger, and Wright mentions during an interview that his firm is acting as an adviser on it. No public announcement has been made. The action by Andrews that is least likely to violate Standard II(A) is:

options.A: notifying all of the firm's investment managers.
options.B: placing the securities on the firm's restricted trading list.
options.C: waiting until the next day to trade.

rationales.A: Andrews should not disclose the information to other managers. Spreading material nonpublic information within the firm widens the group that is barred from trading and invites a violation rather than preventing one; no trading is permitted on material nonpublic information, so notifying managers cannot be justified as a way of keeping clients from being disadvantaged.
rationales.B: The guidance for Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information recommends adding securities to the firm's restricted list when the firm has or may have material nonpublic information. By placing the securities mentioned as part of the merger on that list, Andrews would uphold the standard: the restriction blocks trading in the affected securities by anyone at the firm until the information has been disseminated to the market, which is the control the guidance contemplates.
rationales.C: Waiting until the next day will not ensure that news of the merger is made public. Negotiations may take longer than a day, or the merger may never happen at all; Andrews must wait until the information has been disseminated to the market rather than until an arbitrary time has passed.

questions.stem: During a round of golf, the chief financial officer of Mega Retail tells his long-time friend Hart that the company's quarter will come in almost 10% above estimates. Hart then buys a large stake in a local exchange-traded retail fund rather than in Mega Retail shares. Hart most likely:

options.A: violated Standard II(A) by purchasing the retail fund.
options.B: did not violate Standard II(A), because the information was volunteered.
options.C: did not violate Standard II(A), because he avoided Mega Retail shares.

rationales.A: Hart violated Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information. His decision to invest in the retail fund appears directly correlated with Rodriguez's statement about the successful quarter of Mega Retail. That information is material because it would influence the share price of Mega Retail and would probably influence the price of the entire exchange-traded retail fund, and it was nonpublic. Rodriguez also violated the standard: company officers regularly hold such knowledge about their firms, which is not itself a violation, but sharing it, even in a conversation between friends, is.
rationales.B: The tippee who trades on material nonpublic information violates Standard II(A) in his own right, independently of the tipper's separate breach. That Rodriguez volunteered the earnings information over a round of golf, rather than Hart soliciting it, does not make Hart's investment action permissible.
rationales.C: Material nonpublic information may not be used to trade related instruments either. The prohibition reaches beyond the specific security, and the earnings news would probably influence the price of the whole exchange-traded retail fund, so buying the fund instead of Mega Retail shares does not cure the violation.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), materiality is most likely determined by:

options.A: the substance of the information, regardless of its source.
options.B: substance, specificity, and source reliability.
options.C: the specificity of the information alone.

rationales.A: Materiality does not turn on substance alone. The source, or relative reliability, of the information is itself a determinant of materiality, working alongside substance and specificity. Because the less reliable a source is, the less likely the information it provides will be considered material, two items with identical substance can differ in materiality purely by who supplied them: a statement of fact from a corporate insider about a significant new contract is likely material, while speculation by a competitor about that same contract is likely not.
rationales.B: In addition to the substance and specificity of the information, the source or relative reliability of the information also determines materiality. The less reliable a source, the less likely the information provided would be considered material. Factual information from a corporate insider regarding a significant new contract for a company is likely to be material, whereas an assumption based on speculation by a competitor about the same contract is likely to be less reliable and therefore not material. In the same way, information about trials of a new drug, product, or service under development that comes from qualified personnel involved in those trials is likely to be material, whereas educated conjecture by subject experts not connected to the trials is unlikely to be material. Materiality is therefore a joint test of what the information says, how specific it is, and how reliable its source is.
rationales.C: Specificity alone does not establish materiality. Reliability of the source operates alongside substance and specificity, so information that is highly specific but comes from an unreliable source may still be immaterial. Speculation by a competitor about a contract, or educated conjecture by subject experts not connected to a drug trial, can be quite specific and remain non-material because of where it came from.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), the materiality of information is most likely:

options.A: unchanged however much time has passed since release.
options.B: lower when its price effect is more ambiguous.
options.C: presumed when its price effect is uncertain.

rationales.A: Materiality is not permanent. The passage of time may render information that was once important immaterial, because information loses its capacity to move a price once the market has absorbed it or once events have overtaken it. Materiality has to be assessed as of the moment the information would be used, not fixed at the moment of release.
rationales.B: The more ambiguous the effect of the information on price, the less material that information is considered. If it is unclear whether and to what extent the information will affect the price of a security, the information may not be considered material at all. Materiality tracks expected price impact, so as the link between the information and the price becomes more speculative, the claim to materiality weakens rather than strengthens. The passage of time may also render information that was once important immaterial.
rationales.C: There is no presumption of materiality in the face of uncertainty, and the relationship runs the other way: greater ambiguity about the effect on price makes information less material, not presumptively material. Where it is unclear whether and to what extent the information will affect the price of a security, the information may not be considered material.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), information is most likely considered public once it is:

options.A: available to the marketplace in general.
options.B: disclosed to a closed conference of professional investors.
options.C: shared with anyone outside the issuing company.

rationales.A: Information is nonpublic until it has been disseminated or is available to the marketplace in general, as opposed to a select group of investors. Disseminated can be defined as made known: a company report of profits that is posted on the internet and distributed widely through a press release, or accompanied by a filing, has been effectively disseminated to the marketplace. Members and candidates must have a reasonable expectation that people have received the information before it can be considered public. It is not necessary, however, to wait for the slowest method of delivery.
rationales.B: A closed conference audience, however professional, is a select group of investors rather than the marketplace in general, so the information remains nonpublic. Dissemination requires a reasonable expectation that the market at large has received the information, which a restricted forum does not create no matter how many investors are in the room.
rationales.C: Sharing information beyond the issuing company is not the test. What matters is dissemination to the marketplace in general, so information released to a select group outside the company stays nonpublic; audience size is not itself decisive, since the question is whether the market at large can reasonably be expected to have received it.

questions.stem: Selective disclosure by a corporation to a small group of analysts is most likely to:

options.A: be a concern only if a company insider trades personally.
options.B: render the information public to all investors.
options.C: keep the information nonpublic until general release.

rationales.A: The concern under Standard II(A) is the corporation's communication practice and the recipient's subsequent use of the information, not whether an insider trades for a personal account. Corporations that disclose information on a limited basis create the potential for insider-trading violations by those who receive it, so the issue arises from the selective channel itself and exists whether or not any insider trades.
rationales.B: Disclosure to a small group of analysts or investors is precisely the selective disclosure the guidance warns about, so it does not make the information public. Information that is made available to analysts remains nonpublic until it is made available to investors in general, and a disclosure made to a room full of analysts does not necessarily make the disclosed information public.
rationales.C: Members and candidates must be particularly aware of information that is selectively disclosed by corporations to a small group of investors, analysts, or other market participants. Information that is made available to analysts remains nonpublic until it is made available to investors in general. Corporations that disclose information on a limited basis create the potential for insider-trading violations. Issues of selective disclosure may arise when a corporate insider provides material information to analysts in a briefing or conference call before that information is released to the public, and analysts must be aware that a disclosure made to a room full of analysts does not necessarily make the disclosed information public.

questions.stem: Insider information provided legitimately by a source company under a business agreement is most likely:

options.A: usable for the agreed due diligence.
options.B: usable for personal trading once the deal closes.
options.C: unusable for any purpose.

rationales.A: A member or candidate may use insider information provided legitimately by the source company for the specific purpose of conducting due diligence according to the business agreement between the parties, for such activities as mergers, loan underwriting, credit ratings, and offering engagements. In those instances the investment professional would not be considered in violation of Standard II(A) by using the material information. The permission is tied to the purpose for which the information was supplied: use of insider information provided by the source company for other purposes, especially to trade or to entice others to trade the securities of the firm, is a violation of the standard.
rationales.B: The exception is confined to the agreed diligence purpose, and trading on the information is outside it. Use of insider information provided by the source company for other purposes, especially to trade or to entice others to trade the securities of the firm, violates Standard II(A), and the deal subsequently closing does not cure a trade placed while the information was still material and nonpublic.
rationales.C: Standard II(A) is not absolute on receipt and use. Information provided legitimately by the source company for the specific purpose of conducting due diligence under a business agreement, as in a merger, loan underwriting, credit rating, or offering engagement, may be used for that purpose without violating the standard. What is prohibited is using it for other purposes, particularly trading.

questions.stem: The obligation of a member who obtains material information from a membership-restricted social media group is best described as:

options.A: treating it as public because it was posted online.
options.B: relying on the platform for compliance.
options.C: verifying it is available from a public source.

rationales.A: Appearing on the internet is not the same as being disseminated to the marketplace in general. Some social media platforms require membership in specific groups to access the published content, so information posted there may reach only a select group and may not actually be considered public. Treating anything posted online as public would skip the dissemination test entirely.
rationales.B: The duty sits with the member, not the platform. A member or candidate participating in a group with membership limitations is the one who must verify that material information obtained from that source can also be accessed from a source that would be considered available to the public before using the information; the platform's own policies do not discharge that obligation.
rationales.C: It is important for investment professionals to understand the implications of using information from the internet and social media platforms, because all such information may not actually be considered public. Some social media platforms require membership in specific groups to access the published content. Members and candidates participating in groups with membership limitations should verify that material information obtained from these sources can also be accessed from a source that would be considered available to the public before using that information.

questions.stem: A change in recommendation by a widely respected analyst is most likely:

options.A: material on its own.
options.B: material only once the issuer confirms it.
options.C: never material, being opinion.

rationales.A: When a particularly well-known or respected analyst issues a report or makes changes to his or her recommendation, that information alone may influence the market and thus may be considered material. The analyst is not a company insider, however, and does not have access to inside information. Presumably the analyst created the report from information available to the public, under the mosaic theory, and by using his or her expertise to interpret that information; the analyst's hard work, paid for by the client, generated the conclusions. Simply because the public in general would find the conclusions material does not require that the analyst make the work public. Investors who are not clients can either do the work themselves or become clients to gain access to the analyst's expertise.
rationales.B: Materiality attaches to the expected market impact of the report or recommendation change itself, so confirmation by the issuer is beside the point. The analyst is not a company insider and the conclusions are the analyst's own product, assembled from public information and expertise; the issuer has nothing to confirm.
rationales.C: Being opinion rather than inside fact does not prevent materiality. A particularly well-known or respected analyst's report, or a change in that analyst's recommendation, may by itself influence the market and so may be considered material, even though the analyst holds no inside information and built the conclusions from public information under the mosaic theory.

questions.stem: The mosaic theory is best described by the statement that an analyst:

options.A: may use material public and nonmaterial nonpublic information.
options.B: should use all available and relevant information in a recommendation.
options.C: violates the Code and Standards by not complying with applicable law.

rationales.A: The mosaic theory states that an analyst may use material public information and nonmaterial nonpublic information in creating a larger picture than is shown by any individual piece of information, and that the conclusions the analyst reaches become material only after the pieces are assembled. The permission is what distinguishes the theory: neither input is material nonpublic information on its own, so combining them and acting on the resulting conclusion is appropriate research rather than a violation.
rationales.B: This is an accurate statement about diligence and a reasonable basis under the Code and Standards, but it does not describe the mosaic theory. The mosaic theory is specifically about which categories of information an analyst may combine, namely material public information together with nonmaterial nonpublic information, and about the conclusions becoming material only once assembled.
rationales.C: This is an accurate statement about Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law, which does require members and candidates to know and comply with applicable laws, rules, and regulations. It says nothing about the mosaic theory, which concerns combining material public information with nonmaterial nonpublic information to reach a conclusion.

questions.stem: Under the mosaic theory, an analyst is most likely:

options.A: free to act on conclusions from nonmaterial nonpublic information.
options.B: limited to information that is already public.
options.C: required to disclose the assembled conclusion before acting on it.

rationales.A: A financial analyst gathers and interprets large quantities of information from many sources. The analyst may use significant conclusions derived from the analysis of public and nonmaterial nonpublic information as the basis for investment recommendations and decisions, even if those conclusions would have been material inside information had they been communicated directly to the analyst by a company. Under the mosaic theory, financial analysts are free to act on this collection, or mosaic, of information without risking violation. The source of the conclusion is what matters: it was assembled by the analyst from permitted pieces rather than handed over by an insider.
rationales.B: The mosaic theory expressly permits combining public information with nonmaterial nonpublic information, so the analyst is not confined to what is already public. Nonmaterial nonpublic information may be gathered and interpreted alongside public information, and the significant conclusions drawn from that combination may serve as the basis for investment recommendations and decisions.
rationales.C: No disclosure of the assembled conclusion is required before acting on it. Under the mosaic theory the analyst is free to act on the collection of information even though the same conclusion would have been material inside information had a company communicated it directly to the analyst. The conclusion is the analyst's own product, created from public and nonmaterial nonpublic pieces, and becomes material only once assembled.

questions.stem: The recommended practice for an analyst relying on the mosaic theory is best described as:

options.A: avoiding records that could suggest inside information.
options.B: documenting the research only if a regulator inquires.
options.C: saving and documenting all of the research.

rationales.A: Avoiding records removes the analyst's own best protection. Evidence of the analyst's knowledge of public and nonmaterial nonpublic information about a corporation strengthens the assertion that the analyst reached the conclusions solely through appropriate methods rather than by using material nonpublic information, so documentation supports the mosaic defense rather than undermining it.
rationales.B: Records need to exist as the research is done, not be reconstructed once an inquiry has begun. Contemporaneous evidence of which public and nonmaterial nonpublic pieces the analyst assembled is what supports the assertion that the conclusion was reached through appropriate methods; documentation produced only in response to a regulator carries far less weight.
rationales.C: Although analysts are free to use mosaic information in their research reports, they should save and document all their research. Evidence of the analyst's knowledge of public and nonmaterial nonpublic information about a corporation strengthens the assertion that the analyst reached his or her conclusions solely through appropriate methods rather than through using material nonpublic information. The documentation is what allows the mosaic to be demonstrated after the fact.

questions.stem: A member pays an industry expert through an expert network for insights about a company. Under Standard II(A), the member most likely:

options.A: bears no responsibility once a nondisclosure agreement is signed.
options.B: violates the standard by compensating the expert.
options.C: may compensate the expert without violating the standard.

rationales.A: A signed nondisclosure agreement does not transfer or extinguish the member's duty. Firms connecting experts with members or candidates often require both parties to sign agreements concerning the disclosure of material nonpublic information, but even with the protections of such compliance practices the member remains ultimately responsible for ensuring that he or she is not requesting or acting on confidential information received from an external expert. If the expert does convey material nonpublic information, the member is prohibited from taking investment actions using it until the information becomes publicly known to the market. The agreement allocates obligations between the parties; it does not relieve the member of judging materiality.
rationales.B: Compensation itself is not what the standard prohibits. Standard II(A) guidance states that members and candidates may provide compensation to individuals for their insights without violating the standard. What is prohibited is requesting or acting on confidential information, which may also violate securities regulations. Treating every payment as an implicit solicitation of inside information would rule out expert networks entirely, and the guidance contemplates their legitimate use subject to the member's own diligence.
rationales.C: Members and candidates may provide compensation to individuals for their insights without violating this standard. They remain ultimately responsible, however, for ensuring that they are not requesting or acting on confidential information received from external experts, which may violate securities regulations and would violate the standard. Firms connecting experts with members or candidates often require both parties to sign agreements concerning the disclosure of material nonpublic information. Even with the protections from such compliance practices, if an expert provides material nonpublic information, members and candidates are prohibited from taking investment actions using this information until the information becomes publicly known to the market.

questions.stem: The Standard II(A) prohibition on using material nonpublic information most likely:

options.A: applies only to direct trades in the individual security.
options.B: exempts fixed-income and derivative instruments.
options.C: extends beyond direct trades in individual securities.

rationales.A: The prohibition is not confined to transactions in the security itself. Standard II(A) guidance is explicit that it goes beyond the direct buying and selling of individual securities or bonds: members and candidates must not use material nonpublic information to influence their investment actions related to derivatives, mutual funds, or other alternative investments. Any trading based on material nonpublic information constitutes a violation, so routing the exposure through an indirect instrument does not place the trade outside the standard.
rationales.B: There is no carve-out by asset class. The guidance names individual securities and bonds as the starting point and then extends the prohibition to derivatives, mutual funds, and other alternative investments. Bonds and derivatives are therefore expressly within the scope of the trading prohibition rather than exempt from it, and a member who buys options or redeems a fund holding on the strength of material nonpublic information has violated Standard II(A) just as surely as one who buys the underlying stock.
rationales.C: The prohibition on using this information goes beyond the direct buying and selling of individual securities or bonds. Members and candidates must not use material nonpublic information to influence their investment actions related to derivatives, mutual funds, or other alternative investments. Any trading based on material nonpublic information constitutes a violation of Standard II(A). The operative test is whether the information influenced the investment action, not which instrument was used to express it.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), material information most likely includes:

options.A: earnings, among many other categories.
options.B: reported earnings only.
options.C: only items disclosed in regulatory filings.

rationales.A: Material information may include, but is not limited to, information on the following: earnings; mergers, acquisitions, tender offers, or joint ventures; changes in assets or asset quality; innovative products, processes, or discoveries; new licenses, patents, registered trademarks, or regulatory approval or rejection of a product; developments regarding customers or suppliers, such as the acquisition or loss of a contract; changes in management; change in auditor notification or the fact that the issuer may no longer rely on an auditor's report or qualified opinion; events regarding the issuer's securities, including defaults on senior securities, calls for redemption, repurchase plans, stock splits, dividend changes, changes to the rights of security holders, and public or private sales of additional securities; bankruptcies; significant legal disputes; government reports of economic trends such as employment, housing starts, and currency information; orders for large trades before they are executed; and new or changing equity or debt ratings issued by a third party, such as sell-side recommendations and credit ratings. Earnings open the list, and the list is expressly not exhaustive.
rationales.B: Earnings are only the first item on a long and openly non-exhaustive list. Mergers and acquisitions, changes in asset quality, new patents or regulatory approvals, the gain or loss of a major customer contract, changes in management, a change of auditor, bankruptcies, significant legal disputes, government reports of economic trends, large unexecuted orders, and third-party rating changes all appear alongside it. Confining materiality to reported earnings figures would leave nearly every one of those categories unprotected.
rationales.C: Materiality turns on whether disclosure is likely to affect the price of a security, or on whether reasonable investors would want to know the information before making an investment decision; it does not turn on whether the item has appeared in a regulatory filing. Several of the listed categories are material precisely because they have not yet been filed or announced, including orders for large trades before they are executed and pending mergers, acquisitions, or tender offers. Information already in a filing is generally public and therefore not the concern of Standard II(A) at all.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), the test for whether information is 'material' is most likely:

options.A: a defined regulatory threshold for price movement.
options.B: likely price impact or what reasonable investors would want to know.
options.C: the seniority of the source within the company.

rationales.A: No numeric or regulatory threshold defines materiality. Information is material if its disclosure is likely to have an impact on the price of a security or if reasonable investors would want to know the information before making an investment decision. The specificity of the information, the extent of its difference from public information, its nature, and its reliability are the key factors in that determination, which is a matter of judgement rather than of a bright-line percentage move. A threshold test would also leave information material to a reasonable investor outside the standard whenever the expected price effect happened to fall below the line.
rationales.B: Information is 'material' if its disclosure is likely to have an impact on the price of a security or if reasonable investors would want to know the information before making an investment decision. In other words, information is material if it would significantly alter the total mix of information currently available about a security in such a way that the price of the security would be affected. The two limbs are alternatives, so satisfying either one is enough; the specificity of the information, the extent of its difference from public information, its nature, and its reliability are the key factors in applying them.
rationales.C: Materiality is a function of the content of the information and its likely effect, not of the rank of the person who supplied it. A junior employee, a supplier, a consultant, or an outside expert can all convey information whose disclosure would affect the price or that a reasonable investor would want before deciding, and such information is material. Conversely, a chief executive can pass along something immaterial. Source does bear on reliability, which is one of the assessment factors, but it is not itself the test.

questions.stem: Whether a particular piece of information is material is most likely determined by:

options.A: its specificity, difference from public information, nature, and reliability.
options.B: only its difference from publicly available information.
options.C: a legal determination independent of the information's attributes.

rationales.A: The specificity of the information, the extent of its difference from public information, its nature, and its reliability are key factors in determining whether a particular piece of information fits the definition of material. Vague or general information is less likely to be material than a specific figure; information that merely confirms what the market already knows adds little to the total mix; the nature of the item governs whether a reasonable investor would care about it; and unreliable information is unlikely to move a price. The four factors are applied together rather than ranked.
rationales.B: Difference from public information is one of the four key factors, not the whole test. Specificity and reliability bear on the determination as well, alongside the nature of the information. A rumour that differs sharply from the public record but is vague and of doubtful provenance may well be immaterial, while a precise and reliable figure that refines what is already public may be material. Discarding specificity and reliability would make the assessment turn on novelty alone.
rationales.C: Materiality is not an attribute-blind switch. The specificity of the information, the extent of its difference from public information, its nature, and its reliability are the key factors in determining whether a particular piece of information fits the definition, so the attributes of the information are exactly what the assessment weighs. The conclusion is binary in the sense that information either is or is not material, but reaching it requires judgement about those four characteristics.

questions.stem: Trading or inducing others to trade on material nonpublic information most likely:

options.A: harms only the counterparty to the trade.
options.B: erodes confidence in capital markets and investment professionals.
options.C: improves market efficiency by speeding price discovery.

rationales.A: The damage is systemic rather than bilateral. Trading or inducing others to trade on material nonpublic information erodes confidence in capital markets, institutions, and investment professionals by supporting the idea that those with inside information and special access can take unfair advantage of the general investing public. These actions have caused and will continue to cause investors to avoid capital markets because the markets are perceived to be rigged in favour of the knowledgeable insider. The loss therefore falls on every investor who withdraws, not only on whoever happened to be on the other side of the trade.
rationales.B: Trading or inducing others to trade on material nonpublic information erodes confidence in capital markets, institutions, and investment professionals by supporting the idea that those with inside information and special access can take unfair advantage of the general investing public. Although trading on inside information may lead to short-term profits, in the long run individuals and the profession as a whole suffer from such trading. These actions have caused and will continue to cause investors to avoid capital markets because the markets are perceived to be rigged in favour of the knowledgeable insider, and when the investing public avoids capital markets, markets and capital allocation become less efficient and less supportive of strong and vibrant economies.
rationales.C: Whatever its immediate effect on price, such trading erodes confidence in capital markets, institutions, and investment professionals by rewarding privileged access rather than analytical skill. The guidance draws the opposite conclusion about efficiency: because the investing public comes to see the markets as rigged in favour of the knowledgeable insider and withdraws, markets and capital allocation become less efficient and less supportive of strong and vibrant economies. Short-term profits to the insider do not offset that long-term cost to the profession and to the market.

questions.stem: A company privately gives an analyst guidance interpreting its already published financial statements. That guidance is most likely:

options.A: public information.
options.B: immaterial.
options.C: material nonpublic information.

rationales.A: The underlying financials being public does not make the company's interpretation of them public. Analysts should be alert to the possibility that they are selectively receiving material nonpublic information when a company provides them with guidance or interpretation of such publicly available information as financial statements or regulatory filings. What the analyst now holds is the issuer's own reading of the public record, supplied to a narrow audience and not disseminated to the market, so it is nonpublic even though its subject matter is not.
rationales.B: Interpretive guidance can be material. Even when the underlying information is public, additional interpretation from a company insider may itself constitute material nonpublic information, because it can significantly alter the total mix of information available about the security in a way that would affect the price. An investor relations contact who explains which line item drove a reported result, or how to read a disclosure, may be telling the analyst something a reasonable investor would want to know before deciding.
rationales.C: Analysts should be alert to the possibility that they are selectively receiving material nonpublic information when a company provides them with guidance or interpretation of such publicly available information as financial statements or regulatory filings. Even when the underlying information is public, additional interpretation from a company insider may itself constitute material nonpublic information. The analyst who receives it selectively may not trade or recommend on the basis of it until it has been broadly disseminated to the market, and should encourage the company to make the same disclosure publicly.

questions.stem: FIS's principal owner accepts stock and cash compensation to promote two microcap issuers, then circulates emails, websites, and an online newsletter recommending them. The publications are presented as independent analyses but contain inaccurate, highly promotional, and speculative statements. His conduct most likely:

options.A: did not violate the Code and Standards.
options.B: violated Standard I(C) Misrepresentation only.
options.C: violated Standard II(B) Market Manipulation.

rationales.A: Promotional material dressed as independent research and aimed at inflating a share price is manipulation, and neither a disclaimer nor the theoretical ability of readers to verify the claims cures the deception. The principal owner was paid in stock and cash by the very issuers he recommended, so the independence on which readers relied was false from the outset, and the statements themselves were inaccurate and speculative. A finding of no violation is not available on these facts.
rationales.B: Misrepresentation is engaged, but it does not exhaust the conduct. Using inaccurate reporting and misleading information under the guise of independent analysis in order to raise the price of the promoted stocks is information-based market manipulation, which Standard II(B) addresses directly. The market-integrity standards are precisely the ones aimed at conduct that distorts prices and distorts the market's view of an issuer, so confining the analysis to Standard I(C) understates the breach.
rationales.C: The principal owner of FIS violated Standard II(B) by using inaccurate reporting and misleading information under the guise of independent analysis to artificially increase the stock price of the companies. He was compensated in stock and cash for the promotion, giving him a direct interest in the price he was moving, and he distributed the material through emails, websites, and an online newsletter that presented it as independent work. The inaccurate and highly promotional content, combined with the false appearance of independence, is the information-based manipulation the standard prohibits.

questions.stem: Gray divides his holdings in Fame Pharmaceuticals among multiple accounts in the names of family members, friends, and a religious institution, runs a rumor campaign on blogs and social media, and trades the stock through several brokers on a tactical schedule, selling slightly larger positions than he buys in order to raise volume and price. Gray most likely:

options.A: did not violate Standard II(B).
options.B: violated Standard II(B) through the rumors alone.
options.C: violated Standard II(B) through both the rumors and the trading.

rationales.A: Whose names the accounts carry is irrelevant, because Gray controlled the holdings and directed the trading. He violated Standard II(B) by fraudulently creating the appearance that there was greater investor interest in the stock through the online rumors, and through his trading strategy he created the appearance that there was greater liquidity in the stock than actually existed. Spreading the positions across family members, friends, and a religious institution is what made the circular trading look like genuine market activity, so it aggravates the conduct rather than excusing it.
rationales.B: The rumor campaign is only half of the violation. Buying and selling the stock through multiple brokers on a tactical schedule, and selling slightly larger positions than he bought, manufactured volume and price rather than supplying liquidity to genuine buyers and sellers; the trades were between accounts Gray himself controlled. That created the appearance of greater liquidity in the stock than actually existed, which is transaction-based manipulation under Standard II(B) alongside the information-based manipulation.
rationales.C: Gray violated Standard II(B) by fraudulently creating the appearance that there was greater investor interest in the stock through the online rumors. Additionally, through his trading strategy, he created the appearance that there was greater liquidity in the stock than actually existed. He manipulated the price through both misinformation and trading practices. Dividing the holdings among accounts in the names of family members, friends, and a religious institution disguised the fact that the buying and selling ran between accounts under his own control.

questions.stem: During the quarter-end quiet period, Murphy alerts Divisadero's sales force that his report on Wirewolf is coming. The report's conclusions rest on speculation rather than fact, and he times the release to sensationalize its negative aspects for the distinct advantage of Divisadero's hedge fund clients holding the stock short. Murphy most likely:

options.A: violated Standard II(B) Market Manipulation.
options.B: did not violate the Code and Standards.
options.C: violated Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis only.

rationales.A: Murphy violated Standard II(B) by aiming to create artificial price volatility designed to have a material impact on the price of an issuer's stock. The conclusions rested on speculation rather than fact, he released the report into the thin trading of a quarter-end quiet period, and he shaped the timing to sensationalize the negative findings. The beneficiaries were the hedge fund clients holding the stock short, which supplies the intent: the price movement was the object of the exercise rather than a by-product of research.
rationales.B: Alerting a sales force to forthcoming research can be routine, but these facts are not. Murphy's conclusions were speculative rather than factual, and he chose the quarter-end quiet period and a sensationalized presentation in order to move the price for the benefit of clients positioned short. Conduct aimed at creating artificial price volatility with a material impact on an issuer's stock is market manipulation whatever the ordinary practice around pre-release notice may be.
rationales.C: The speculative basis is a genuine diligence failing, but it does not account for the whole of the conduct. What makes this a Standard II(B) matter is the manipulative purpose: Murphy aimed to create artificial price volatility designed to have a material impact on the price of the issuer's stock, timing and framing the release so that Divisadero's short-holding hedge fund clients would profit. Treating it as a reasonable-basis problem alone leaves the intent to distort the price unaddressed.

questions.stem: Sekar manages two funds, one of which holds an excessive position in Digital Design (DD), a stock with low liquidity. He decides to trade larger portions of DD back and forth between his two funds in order to raise the price slowly so that other market participants become interested. Sekar's plan most likely:

options.A: complies with Standard II(B), because fund participants benefit.
options.B: violates Standard II(B) by distorting DD's volume and price.
options.C: complies with Standard II(B), because the trades are internal rebalancing.

rationales.A: Benefit to the funds' participants does not excuse the method. The plan works only by artificially distorting both the trading volume and the price of a thinly traded stock, and any improvement in DD's apparent liquidity would be an artifact of Sekar's own cross trades rather than genuine outside interest. Standard II(B) Market Manipulation turns on the intent to mislead market participants, and Sekar's stated intent is to move the price so that others take an interest.
rationales.B: Sekar's plan would be beneficial for his funds' participants, but it is based on artificial distortion of both the trading volume and the price of the DD stock and thus constitutes a violation of Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. Because DD is illiquid, repeated round trips between the two funds create the impression of activity and price movement that does not reflect any genuine change in supply or demand, which is a diversion from the expectations of a fair and efficient market.
rationales.C: Internal rebalancing between funds under common management is not objectionable in itself, but these are not rebalancing trades. They are repeated round trips in the same security, sized and timed to push the quoted price higher. Transactions that result in no real change in beneficial ownership are a listed indicator of manipulation, and the standard reaches any trade that distorts the market's picture of volume or price, whoever holds both sides of it.

questions.stem: Gordon publishes earnings projections for Hygene that run $0.15 to $2.15 above company guidance, exaggerating them to push the company into updating its guidance and to fuel a quick gain for her momentum-style clients. Gordon most likely:

options.A: violates Standard II(B) by exaggerating her projections.
options.B: violates no standard, because she believes the outcome possible.
options.C: violates Standard II(A) by using nonpublic information.

rationales.A: By exaggerating her earnings projections in order to try to fuel a quick gain in Hygene's stock price, Gordon is in violation of Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. This is information-based manipulation: the projections are not her honest estimate but a device to pressure the company into revising guidance and to move the price for her momentum-style clients. It would have been acceptable for Gordon to write a report that (1) framed her earnings projection as a range of possible outcomes and (2) clearly outlined the assumptions used in her Hygene models, including the findings from her trip through Latin America.
rationales.B: A genuinely held, well-supported estimate may sit far from company guidance, and an analyst is free to publish it. What fails here is intent: Gordon deliberately exaggerated the figures to force a guidance update and fuel a quick gain, so the report functions as a tool for moving the price rather than as an honest forecast. Believing an outcome to be remotely possible does not cure the manipulative purpose.
rationales.C: No material nonpublic information is involved. Gordon's inputs are her own models and her own travel observations, not inside information obtained from Hygene, so Standard II(A) is not engaged. The breach is information-based manipulation under Standard II(B).

questions.stem: Weinberg logs on to several investor chatrooms and starts rumors that Moosehead & Belfast Railroad is about to expand its rail network in anticipation of a large lumber contract. Weinberg most likely:

options.A: violates Standard II(B) by disseminating false information.
options.B: violates no standard, because chatroom posts are speculation.
options.C: violates Standard II(A) by trading on nonpublic information.

rationales.A: Weinberg violated Standard II(B) Market Manipulation by disseminating false information about Moosehead & Belfast with the intent to mislead market participants. Spreading false rumors to induce trading by others is the classic form of information-based manipulation: pumping up the price of an investment with misleading positive information, then dumping the position once other participants have driven the price to an artificially high level.
rationales.B: The venue does not change the analysis. Standard II(B) prohibits disseminating false or misleading information with the intent to mislead market participants wherever it is published, and the skepticism of a chatroom audience is no defense for a rumor the poster knows to be fabricated.
rationales.C: There is no inside information here. Weinberg invented the rail-network expansion and the lumber contract rather than learning of them from the issuer, so nothing material and nonpublic has been misused and Standard II(A) is not engaged. The violation is market manipulation under Standard II(B).

questions.stem: Pietro's firm, Local Bank, is looking for a merger partner, but potential buyers are holding back in the expectation that next period's data will be worse. Pietro most likely violates the Standards by:

options.A: placing a personal buy order many times the average weekly volume.
options.B: instructing a press release announcing that the bank has retained Vogt.
options.C: instructing a release reaffirming the firm's prior earnings guidance.

rationales.A: Pietro places a buy order for 2,000 shares, four times the average weekly volume, through Vogt for his personal account. Through placing a personal purchase order that is significantly greater than the average volume, Pietro is violating Standard II(B) Market Manipulation. He is attempting to manipulate an increase in the share price and thus bring a buyer to the negotiating table. The news of a possible merger and confirmation of the firm's earnings guidance may also have positive effects on the price of Local Bank, but Pietro's actions in instructing the release of that information do not represent a violation through market manipulation.
rationales.B: Announcing that the bank has retained Vogt is accurate information about a real engagement, and announcements of this nature are common and practical to keep investors informed. The announcement may well lift the price, but a truthful disclosure that happens to be favorable is not manipulation. The violation lies in the oversized personal buy order.
rationales.C: Reaffirming guidance the firm has already given is likewise accurate information released to keep investors informed, and such releases are common and practical. Any positive effect on the price of Local Bank does not convert the release into market manipulation. The violation lies in the oversized personal buy order.

questions.stem: Information-based manipulation under Standard II(B) is most likely to:

options.A: require proof that the member profited from the rumor.
options.B: include spreading false rumors to induce trading by others.
options.C: apply only to trades executed on a regulated exchange.

rationales.A: Profit is not an element of the offense. Standard II(B) is breached by disseminating information with the intent to mislead market participants; whether the scheme worked, and whether the member made money from it, bears on the damage done but not on whether the standard was violated.
rationales.B: Information-based manipulation includes, but is not limited to, spreading false rumors to induce trading by others. Members and candidates must refrain from pumping up the price of an investment by issuing misleading positive information or overly optimistic projections of a security's worth only to later dump the investment, that is, sell it, once the price, fueled by the misleading information's effect on other market participants, reaches an artificially high level.
rationales.C: The prohibition is not venue-specific. It applies wherever the information is disseminated and wherever the resulting trading takes place, including over-the-counter markets and private transactions.

questions.stem: Transaction-based manipulation under Standard II(B) is most likely to:

options.A: require proof that prices actually moved as a result of the trades.
options.B: involve actions the member knows or should know could distort prices.
options.C: cover only trades executed through undisclosed nominee accounts.

rationales.A: Realized price impact is not the test. It is enough that the member or candidate knows, or should know, that the actions could distort the price of a security, so an attempt that fails to move the market still falls within the standard.
rationales.B: Transaction-based manipulation involves instances where a member or candidate knows or should know that his or her actions could distort the price of a security. This type of manipulation includes, but is not limited to: (1) transactions that artificially affect prices or volume to give the impression of activity or price movement in a financial instrument, which represent a diversion from the expectations of a fair and efficient market; and (2) securing a controlling, dominant position in a financial instrument in order to exploit and manipulate the price of a related derivative or of the underlying asset.
rationales.C: Nominee accounts are not the defining feature. The category reaches any volume- or price-distorting transaction however it is executed, including wash trades in the member's own name, cross trades between funds under common management, and the accumulation of a dominant position used to move a related derivative.

questions.stem: With respect to legitimate trading strategies, Standard II(B) is most likely to:

options.A: permit transactions based on perceived market inefficiencies.
options.B: treat exploiting a perceived inefficiency as manipulation.
options.C: presume a violation where a strategy produces unusually high volume.

rationales.A: Standard II(B) is not intended to preclude transactions undertaken on legitimate trading strategies based on perceived market inefficiencies. Legitimate trading activity may appear abusive, especially where the market is illiquid or volatile, so appearance alone settles nothing. The intent of the action is critical to determining whether it is a violation of this standard.
rationales.B: Trading to exploit a perceived mispricing is ordinary active management and is the mechanism by which prices are corrected. The standard is aimed at distorting prices or volumes in order to mislead other participants, not at profiting from a view that those participants are wrong.
rationales.C: Volume alone is not the test, and legitimate activity can easily look abusive where the market is illiquid or volatile. The critical element is the intent of the action, not the size of the footprint it leaves.

questions.stem: An indicator that may signal market manipulation under Standard II(B) is most likely:

options.A: a large block trade executed to meet a client's genuine liquidity need.
options.B: the dissemination of accurate research that moves a security's price.
options.C: an order entered for an unusually short time period.

rationales.A: Trading to meet a client's genuine liquidity need is legitimate activity, however large the block. Size can make legitimate trading look abusive in a thin market, but the indicator list is aimed at order patterns that serve no purpose other than to shift prices or to create the appearance of activity.
rationales.B: Publishing factual information is permitted even if prices move in response. Information-based manipulation requires false or misleading information disseminated with the intent to mislead market participants; accurate research that the market acts on is the opposite of that.
rationales.C: Orders entered for an unusually short time period appear on the nonexhaustive list of indicators that may signal market manipulation. The others are: orders above market price; orders resulting in no change in beneficial ownership; orders that intend to change the bid or offer prices and are canceled before they are executed; orders on both sides of the trade using different platforms; and coordinated action by two or more traders in a market with a small number of participants.

questions.stem: Market manipulation most likely damages:

options.A: no one.
options.B: only unsophisticated retail investors.
options.C: all investors.

rationales.A: Prices may revert, but the harm does not. Manipulation disrupts the smooth functioning of financial markets and lowers investor confidence while it persists, and the resulting loss of trust in the fairness of the markets outlasts the price distortion itself.
rationales.B: The damage is not confined to the manipulator's counterparties. A lack of trust in the fairness of the capital markets raises risk premiums and reduces participation for every investor, sophisticated and institutional investors included.
rationales.C: Market manipulation damages the interests of all investors by disrupting the smooth functioning of financial markets and lowering investor confidence. Market manipulation may lead to a lack of trust in the fairness of the capital markets, resulting in higher risk premiums and reduced investor participation. A reduction in the efficiency of a local capital market may negatively affect the growth and economic health of the country and may also influence the operations of the globally interconnected capital markets.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), a member who possesses material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment is most likely:

options.A: free to trade once others appear to have acted on the information.
options.B: permitted to act after sharing the information with all clients.
options.C: barred from acting on the information or causing others to act.

rationales.A: Another party's misuse of the information does not release the member. The prohibition runs until the information has been disseminated to the marketplace; a belief that someone else has already traded neither makes the information public nor cures the member's own breach.
rationales.B: Distributing material nonpublic information to clients so that they can trade on it is causing others to act on the information, which the standard prohibits in the same breath as acting on it oneself. Treating clients equally is a fair-dealing concern and does nothing to make the information public.
rationales.C: Members and candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information. The duty is absolute while the information remains nonpublic: the member may neither trade for client accounts nor for a personal account, nor pass the information to anyone who might trade on it, and the restriction lifts only once the information has been publicly disseminated.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(B), the prohibition on market manipulation is best described as:

options.A: barring both price distortion and artificial volume inflation intended to mislead.
options.B: permitting price distortion if the strategy is disclosed to the exchange in advance.
options.C: barring artificial volume inflation but not price distortion.

rationales.A: Standard II(B) provides that members and candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants. Both limbs are covered: manipulation of the reported price or value of a security, and manipulation of its apparent liquidity. The operative test is the intent to mislead, so genuine, economically motivated transactions are not caught, while wash trades, matched orders, and order entry designed to create a false impression of activity are.
rationales.B: Disclosure does not authorize practices intended to mislead market participants. Notifying the exchange in advance neither removes the intent nor protects the participants whose trading decisions the distorted prices would corrupt. Standard II(B) prohibits the conduct outright rather than conditioning it on notice, so a disclosed manipulation is still a manipulation.
rationales.C: Both price distortion and artificial volume inflation undertaken with intent to mislead are prohibited. Reading the standard as reaching volume alone would leave the more direct abuse permitted, namely setting a false price, which is the core of market manipulation and the first practice the standard names.

questions.stem: A member trades on material nonpublic information and loses money on the trade. Under Standard II(A), the loss is most likely:

options.A: no defense to the violation.
options.B: a complete defense, since no advantage was gained.
options.C: grounds for treating the breach as a record-keeping infraction.
