rationales.A: The fact that a member or candidate lost money on a trade based on material nonpublic information does not absolve the member or candidate of trading on that information. Standard II(A) prohibits acting, or causing others to act, on material nonpublic information, so liability attaches at execution and does not depend on the outcome. It is the member's or candidate's responsibility to establish, before executing any investment action, that what was heard, such as comments about earnings, is not material nonpublic information. A member who bought on an insider's earnings remark and then watched the shares fall has still violated the standard.
rationales.B: The violation is acting on the information, not profiting from it. A trade's outcome is set by the market after the order is placed and says nothing about whether the member held an informational advantage over other participants at the moment of the trade. A rule that excused losing trades would let members act on every tip and invoke the standard only when it paid off.
rationales.C: There is no downgrade mechanism in Standard II(A). The prohibition runs to the act of trading, or inducing others to trade, on material nonpublic information, so neither the size nor the sign of the result reclassifies the breach, and the standard imposes no record-keeping requirement that a loss could convert the matter into.

drills.los_text: recommend practices and procedures designed to prevent violations of the Code and Standards
drills.reading_name: Guidance for Standard II: Integrity of Capital Markets

questions.stem: A member obtains material nonpublic information about a company she follows. Under Standard II(A), her recommended course of action is most likely to:

options.A: make reasonable efforts to achieve public dissemination.
options.B: wait quietly for the information to become stale before resuming coverage.
options.C: destroy the information and tell no one.

rationales.A: If a member or candidate obtains material nonpublic information, the member or candidate should make reasonable efforts to achieve public dissemination of the information. Those efforts usually entail encouraging the issuing company to make the information public. If public dissemination is not possible, the member or candidate must communicate the information only to the designated supervisory and compliance personnel within the firm and must not take investment action or alter current investment recommendations on the basis of it. Members and candidates must also not knowingly engage in any conduct that may induce company insiders to disclose material nonpublic information privately.
rationales.B: Passive waiting is not the guidance. Doing nothing leaves the information selectively held, leaves other market participants trading against someone who knows more, and still leaves the member unable to act or publish until disclosure occurs. The guidance calls for affirmative efforts at dissemination, coupled with communication to designated supervisory and compliance personnel where dissemination cannot be achieved.
rationales.C: Destroying the information and saying nothing suppresses what the market needs and bypasses the firm's compliance function. The recommended course is to make reasonable efforts to achieve public dissemination, typically by encouraging the company to release it, and where that fails to route the information internally to designated supervisory and compliance personnel while taking no investment action on it.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), an employer's compliance procedures for preventing the misuse of material nonpublic information are best described as:

options.A: binding on supervisors but not on the analysts and managers they oversee.
options.B: binding on every member and candidate at the firm.
options.C: advisory, so members may deviate when their own judgment differs.

rationales.A: The compliance duty applies to every member and candidate at the firm, not only to those with supervisory responsibility. Procedures such as review of employee and proprietary trading, review of investment recommendations, and watch lists are written precisely to reach the analysts and portfolio managers who handle issuer information day to day, so a duty limited to supervisors would leave the people closest to the information unbound.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must comply with all compliance procedures adopted by their employer to prevent the misuse of material nonpublic information. Such procedures might address areas including the review of employee and proprietary trading, the review of investment recommendations, the supervision of interdepartmental communications in multiservice firms, and the informing of compliance personnel of suspected inappropriate use of material nonpublic information.
rationales.C: Compliance with employer procedures adopted to prevent the misuse of material nonpublic information is mandatory, not advisory. Allowing each member to substitute personal judgment for the firm's procedure would defeat the firm-wide consistency on which firewalls, watch lists, and clearance requirements depend, since a single unilateral exception is enough to move the information across the wall.

questions.stem: Standard II(A) recommends practices that reduce the risk of selective disclosure at analyst meetings. The practice members and candidates should follow is most likely to:

options.A: discourage press releases ahead of analyst calls so the calls retain news value.
options.B: leave the scripting of analyst meetings to the company alone.
options.C: encourage pre-meeting press releases and the scripting of analyst meetings.

rationales.A: Members and candidates should encourage pre-call press releases rather than discourage them. Releasing the material before the meeting is what makes the information public ahead of the discussion, and preserving a call's news value is the opposite of the objective, because that value consists of exactly the selective advantage the standard seeks to remove.
rationales.B: Encouraging companies to script analyst meetings and conference calls is part of the recommended practice, not an intrusion into the company's internal affairs. A script limits improvised answers that stray into undisclosed material information, so the analyst has a legitimate interest in urging it and the guidance says so explicitly.
rationales.C: Members and candidates should encourage companies they follow to issue press releases prior to analyst meetings and conference calls, and to script those meetings and calls to decrease the chance that further information will be disclosed. If material nonpublic information is disclosed for the first time in an analyst meeting or call, members and candidates should encourage the company to issue a press release promptly or otherwise make the information publicly available. Both halves of the practice serve the same end: the information reaches every market participant at once rather than reaching the people in the room first.

questions.stem: A multiservice firm has both investment banking and brokerage operations. To prevent violations of Standard II(A), its best policy is most likely to:

options.A: erect physical and informational barriers between the two operations.
options.B: monitor the exchange of information between the two operations.
options.C: prohibit buy and sell recommendations on investment banking clients permanently.

rationales.A: The best policy to prevent violation of Standard II(A) is the establishment of firewalls within the firm to prevent the exchange of insider information. The physical and informational barrier of a firewall between the investment banking department and the brokerage operation prevents the banking department from providing information to analysts on the brokerage side who may be writing recommendations on a company's stock. Prohibiting recommendations is an alternative but a blunter one, and monitoring is weaker still, because no exchange of information should be taking place for the firm to monitor.
rationales.B: No exchange of information should be occurring between the investment banking department and the brokerage operation, so monitoring such exchanges is not an effective compliance procedure for preventing the use of material nonpublic information. Monitoring documents a flow the firm should have prevented and detects the breach only after the information has already crossed; a barrier stops the crossing itself.
rationales.C: A permanent prohibition goes further than necessary. Once an offering is complete and the material nonpublic information obtained by the investment banking department becomes public, resuming the publication of recommendations on the stock is not a violation of the Code and Standards, so a permanent ban needlessly deprives brokerage clients of research on those companies.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), the elements of an effective firewall system are best described as including:

options.A: control of interdepartmental communications through a clearance area.
options.B: free-flowing interdepartmental communication, logged after the fact.
options.C: physical separation of departments and nothing further.

rationales.A: Elements of such a system include, but are not limited to, the following: substantial control of relevant interdepartmental communications, preferably through a clearance area within the firm in either the compliance or the legal department; review of employee trading through the maintenance of watch, restricted, and rumor lists; documentation of the procedures designed to limit the flow of information between departments and of the actions taken to enforce those procedures; and heightened review or restriction of proprietary trading while the firm is in possession of material nonpublic information.
rationales.B: Relevant communications are substantially controlled, preferably through a clearance area in the compliance or legal department, rather than left to flow freely with a retrospective log. A log tells the firm after the fact that information crossed the wall, whereas the point of a clearance area is that nothing crosses without prior review and approval.
rationales.C: Physical separation is one element among several. The system also requires control of relevant communications through a clearance area, review of employee trading through watch, restricted, and rumor lists, documentation of the procedures and of the actions taken to enforce them, and heightened review or restriction of proprietary trading while the firm holds material nonpublic information.

questions.stem: A multiservice firm maintains a firewall between its investment banking and research departments. Under Standard II(A), its staffing of those departments is most likely such that:

options.A: no employee sits on both sides of the firewall at any time.
options.B: employees rotate between the two sides when projects do not overlap in time.
options.C: only junior employees are confined to one side of the firewall.

rationales.A: There should be no overlap of personnel between the investment banking and corporate finance areas of a brokerage firm and the sales and research departments, or between a bank's commercial lending department and its trust and research departments. For a firewall to be effective in a multiservice firm, an employee should be on only one side of the firewall at any time, because a person sitting on both sides is a channel through which issuer information passes without ever being deliberately sent anywhere.
rationales.B: Staggering the work does not cure the problem. The restriction is on an employee being on both sides of the wall, and information learned on the banking side remains material and nonpublic until it is publicly disclosed, which is not the same event as a project closing. Non-overlapping projects therefore still place the same undisclosed knowledge inside the research department.
rationales.C: The no-overlap principle is not seniority-based. A senior officer spanning both sides defeats the barrier as surely as a junior analyst would, and typically holds more of the sensitive information, so the requirement that an employee be on only one side at any time applies to everyone the wall divides.

questions.stem: A multiservice firm's investment banking department is working on a deal with a company covered by one of the firm's research analysts. Under Standard II(A), that analyst is most likely:

options.A: barred from providing any assistance to the investment banking department.
options.B: permitted to provide limited assistance under controlled circumstances.
options.C: free of restrictions once the deal is complete.

rationales.A: Limited assistance is permitted under carefully controlled circumstances, so an absolute bar overstates the restriction. What the standard controls is the consequence of helping rather than the helping itself: the analyst crosses to the investment banking side and must stay there until the information learned is publicly disclosed.
rationales.B: An analyst who follows a particular company may provide limited assistance to the investment bankers under carefully controlled circumstances when the firm's investment banking department is involved in a deal with the company. That analyst must then be treated as though he or she were an investment banker and must remain on the investment banking side of the wall until any information he or she learns is publicly disclosed. In short, the analyst cannot use any information learned in the course of the project for research purposes and cannot share that information with colleagues in the research department.
rationales.C: The analyst is treated as a banking-side participant and remains restricted until the information learned becomes public, which is not the same moment as the end of the project. A deal can close, or be abandoned, while the information it generated is still undisclosed; until disclosure the analyst may neither use that information in research nor pass it to research colleagues.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), the primary objective of an effective firewall procedure is most likely to:

options.A: eliminate all communication between departments permanently.
options.B: leave cross-departmental communications to be reviewed by the requesting employees.
options.C: establish a reporting system in which authorized people approve communications.

rationales.A: The objective is a reporting system in which authorized personnel review and approve necessary communications between departments, not a total and permanent ban. Multiservice firms sometimes must move information across the wall, the clearest case being an analyst drawn onto a deal, and the procedure exists to make that passage controlled, approved, and documented rather than impossible.
rationales.B: Review and approval sit with designated compliance personnel, not with the employees asking to share the information. Those employees have an interest in the transfer and no independent vantage point from which to weigh it, so self-approval would leave the firewall without the control that gives it force.
rationales.C: A primary objective of an effective firewall procedure is to establish a reporting system in which authorized people review and approve communications between departments. If an employee behind a firewall believes he or she needs to share confidential information with someone on the other side, the employee should consult a designated compliance officer to determine whether the sharing is necessary and how much information should be shared. If the sharing is necessary, the compliance officer should coordinate the process of looking over the wall so that the necessary information is shared and the integrity of the procedure is maintained.

questions.stem: With respect to employees' personal trading, Standard II(A) most likely requires members and candidates to:

options.A: treat personal trades as private and outside employer oversight.
options.B: comply with their employer's restrictions on personal trading.
options.C: observe restrictions only for securities on the firm's restricted list.

rationales.A: Personal accounts are not a zone of privacy beyond the employer's compliance reach. Members and candidates must comply with their employers' restrictions or prohibitions on personal trading by employees, and the compliance practices contemplated under Standard II(A) reach directly into those accounts: firm monitoring of personal trading, mandated periodic reports of personal transactions, and restricted lists and watch lists of companies. Treating personal trades as outside employer oversight would defeat the very mechanism the standard relies on to keep material nonpublic information from being exploited through an employee's own account.
rationales.B: Members and candidates must comply with their employers' restrictions or prohibitions on personal trading by employees. Such practices may include firm monitoring of personal trading, mandating periodic reports of personal transactions, and implementing a restricted list and watch list of companies. Compliance with those employer limitations is the member's part of the firm's control framework over material nonpublic information: the firm builds the monitoring and reporting apparatus, and the member is obliged to operate inside it rather than to judge for himself or herself which personal transactions matter.
rationales.C: Employer limitations, monitoring, and periodic reporting extend to personal trading generally, not only to names already on the firm's restricted list. The restricted list is one tool among several named in the guidance, alongside firm monitoring of personal trading, mandated periodic reports of personal transactions, and a watch list. A member who complied only as to restricted-list securities would still be disregarding the employer's broader restrictions and reporting requirements, and so would still fall short of Standard II(A).

questions.stem: Standard II(A) guidance on a firm's restricted list most likely describes the list as:

options.A: a reactive tool, used once an insider-trading inquiry has begun.
options.B: a preventive tool, used when the firm may have material nonpublic information.
options.C: a discouraged tool, because it signals that the firm holds such information.

rationales.A: The restricted list is preventive rather than reactive. The guidance recommends adding securities to it when the firm has or may have material nonpublic information, which is well before any inquiry, investigation, or enforcement interest arises. Waiting for an insider-trading inquiry to begin would mean the firm had already traded or issued recommendations during the period it held the information, so the list would be documenting a violation rather than preventing one.
rationales.B: The guidance for Standard II(A) recommends adding securities to the firm's restricted list when the firm has or may have material nonpublic information. By adding these securities to the list, a member or candidate upholds the standard. Note the breadth of the trigger: "has or may have" means the member does not need to have confirmed either that the information is in the firm's hands or that it is material before acting. The restricted list is one of the tools that prevents both trading and the issuance of recommendations while the firm holds such information, and it works precisely because it is applied early and conservatively.
rationales.C: Adding securities to the restricted list when the firm has or may have material nonpublic information is the recommended practice, not a discouraged one. Restricted lists are a standard element of a multiservice firm's controls, used in combination with information barriers, watch lists, and monitoring of personal and proprietary trading. A firm that declined to maintain one for fear of signalling its position would be left with no mechanism to stop trading and recommendations in the affected security.

questions.stem: An information barrier, commonly called a firewall, is most likely:

options.A: an approach largely abandoned as unenforceable.
options.B: a barrier between the firm and its regulators.
options.C: the most widely used means of containing material nonpublic information.

rationales.A: The information barrier, commonly referred to as a firewall, remains the most widely used approach for preventing the communication of material nonpublic information within firms. Electronic communication raises the demands on a barrier rather than retiring it: the barrier is implemented through access controls on systems and files, physical and reporting separation of departments, review of interdepartmental communication, and documented procedures for crossing the barrier when a legitimate need arises. It has not fallen out of use.
rationales.B: A firewall restricts the interdepartmental flow of material nonpublic information inside the firm, directing confidential information only to those who need to know it to perform their jobs effectively. It has nothing to do with the firm's communication with regulators, which is unaffected and in many circumstances compulsory. Mischaracterizing the barrier as a shield against regulators inverts its purpose, which is to protect the integrity of capital markets rather than to withhold information from oversight.
rationales.C: An information barrier commonly referred to as a firewall is the most widely used approach for preventing the communication of material nonpublic information within firms. It restricts the flow of confidential information to those who need to know the information to perform their jobs effectively. In a multiservice firm, where an investment banking department may legitimately hold information that the research and trading departments must not act on, the barrier is what allows the two sides of the business to coexist, and it is normally supported by restricted lists, watch lists, and surveillance of trading and personal accounts.

questions.stem: If public dissemination of material nonpublic information is not possible, Standard II(A) most likely requires the member to:

options.A: report it only to designated supervisory and compliance personnel and take no investment action.
options.B: trade on it after documenting the failed attempt at dissemination.
options.C: circulate it to all of the firm's portfolio managers.

rationales.A: If public dissemination is not possible, the member or candidate must communicate the information only to the designated supervisory and compliance personnel within the member's or candidate's firm and must not take investment action or alter current investment recommendations based on the information. Both halves of that obligation bind at once: the information is contained within the smallest group able to act on it in a compliance capacity, and the member's own investment conduct freezes. Withdrawing or changing a current recommendation is itself a form of acting on the information, which is why the standard reaches alterations to existing recommendations and not only new trades.
rationales.B: When dissemination cannot be achieved, the member must not take investment action or alter current investment recommendations based on the information. Documentation does not restore trading freedom; an attempt to make the information public, however diligent, does not change the fact that the market still does not have it. Trading at that point is exactly the conduct Standard II(A) prohibits, and a contemporaneous memo recording the attempt would serve only as evidence of knowledge.
rationales.C: The information goes only to the designated supervisory and compliance personnel within the firm. Broad circulation to the firm's portfolio managers multiplies the violation rather than equalizing it, because each recipient then holds material nonpublic information and is barred from acting, and the firm loses any ability to contain the information or to document who knew what. Fairness among clients is not achieved by spreading the information internally; it is achieved by the firm trading on none of it until the information is public.

questions.stem: With respect to inducing company insiders to privately disclose material nonpublic information, Standard II(A) most likely prohibits:

options.A: only inducement for which the insider is compensated.
options.B: only a direct request for the information.
options.C: any conduct that may knowingly induce such disclosure.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must not knowingly engage in any conduct that may induce company insiders to privately disclose material nonpublic information. Nothing in that formulation turns on whether value changes hands. Compensation may aggravate the conduct and may raise separate issues under other standards, but an uncompensated encouragement that is designed to draw out private disclosure is squarely within the prohibition.
rationales.B: The prohibition covers any conduct that may induce company insiders to privately disclose material nonpublic information, not merely an explicit request for it. Conduct that steers an insider toward selective disclosure, such as framing questions so that a confirmation or a refusal is itself informative, or cultivating an insider relationship in order to elicit detail that has not been made public, falls within the standard even though no direct request was ever made.
rationales.C: Members and candidates must not knowingly engage in any conduct that may induce company insiders to privately disclose material nonpublic information. This duty sits within the achieve public dissemination compliance practice: a member who learns of possibly material nonpublic information should encourage the issuer to make it public, and must not work in the opposite direction by drawing private disclosure out of insiders. The breadth of the language is deliberate, reaching conduct that may induce disclosure rather than only conduct that succeeds in doing so.

questions.stem: For material information obtained from a social media group with membership limitations, Standard II(A) most likely directs members and candidates to:

options.A: avoid joining such groups.
options.B: treat the information as public.
options.C: verify that it is also publicly available before using it.

rationales.A: Participation in groups with membership limitations is acceptable; the duty the guidance imposes is verification, not abstention. Members and candidates may belong to such groups and may use what they find there, provided they first establish that material information obtained from those sources can also be accessed from a source that would be considered available to the public. Avoiding the groups entirely is not what the standard asks and would not improve a member's compliance.
rationales.B: Material information obtained from a group with membership limitations cannot be assumed to be public merely because its members are numerous or because any of them could repost it. Members and candidates participating in such groups should verify that the information can also be accessed from a source that would be considered available to the public before using it. Until that verification is done, the information is restricted in fact, and acting on it exposes the member to the prohibition on trading or recommending on the basis of material nonpublic information.
rationales.C: Members and candidates participating in groups with membership limitations should verify that material information obtained from these sources can also be accessed from a source that would be considered available to the public before using that information. The test is the availability of the information to the investing public, not the size or informality of the forum in which the member encountered it, and the verification must precede any use of the information, whether in trading or in a recommendation.

questions.stem: An analyst who obtains information through an expert network is most likely required to:

options.A: assess its materiality independently of any signed agreement.
options.B: rely on the participants' agreements that no such information was conveyed.
options.C: leave the materiality assessment to the network operator.

rationales.A: An analyst cannot simply rely on the agreements signed by individuals who participate in expert networks stating that he or she has not received information that would prohibit trading activity. The analyst must make his or her own determination whether information received through these arrangements reaches a materiality threshold that would influence his or her trading. The reason is that the person signing the agreement is not the person who knows how the information would be used: a detail an industry participant regards as routine may be decisive for a specific position, and only the analyst can judge that.
rationales.B: A signed agreement does not transfer the analyst's duty. The analyst cannot simply rely on agreements signed by expert-network participants stating that no information prohibiting trading was conveyed; each piece of information received must be independently assessed for materiality. The agreement records the participant's understanding of what was permitted, which is evidence of good process but not a finding about what was actually said or about how material it is to the analyst's investment decision.
rationales.C: The duty to assess materiality rests with the analyst who receives the information and would act on it, not with the network operator. The operator's screening, consent forms, and call protocols are controls on the arrangement, and the analyst may welcome them, but they do not substitute for the analyst's own determination whether what was said reaches a materiality threshold that would influence his or her trading.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(B), a firm's procedures against manipulative trading most likely address:

options.A: orders placed and canceled with intent to deceive.
options.B: manipulative trades only once they are executed.
options.C: neither order entry nor order cancellation patterns.

rationales.A: Members and candidates must comply with their firm's policies and procedures designed to prevent manipulative trading, which could include procedures designed to prevent placing and canceling orders with the intent to deceive others into buying or selling securities at artificial prices. The deception in that pattern lies in the displayed order itself, which misrepresents supply or demand to other market participants, so the procedures have to reach the order message and not merely the fill.
rationales.B: Deceptive order entry is covered even when the orders never execute. An order placed and then canceled with the intent to deceive others into buying or selling at artificial prices has already conveyed a false signal about supply and demand to the market, and the absence of a fill does not undo that. Procedures limited to executed trades would miss the conduct entirely, which is why the compliance practices named under Standard II(B) include preventing the placing and canceling of such orders.
rationales.C: Placing and canceling orders with intent to deceive, as in spoofing or layering, is manipulative conduct that the firm's procedures are expected to target. It is not outside compliance's remit for want of an execution: the practices named under Standard II(B) include procedures designed to prevent such order entry, real-time monitoring and systematic surveillance for suspicious order entries across platforms, and automated order management with pretrade controls, all of which operate on order activity rather than on completed trades.

questions.stem: The surveillance practice recommended under Standard II(B) is most likely:

options.A: real-time monitoring across multiple trading platforms.
options.B: reliance on self-regulatory organizations' monitoring.
options.C: end-of-day exception reports on the firm's primary venue.

rationales.A: The recommended practice is real-time monitoring or systematic surveillance across multiple platforms, designed to identify such activities as suspicious order entries, potential improper coordination among customers, wash trading, transactions in cross-product securities that manipulate the price of an underlying security, and other types of manipulative trading activity. Both features matter. Monitoring has to be contemporaneous, because an order that is placed and canceled to move a price is gone before a batch report is produced, and it has to span platforms, because coordination and cross-product manipulation are visible only when activity in related venues and instruments is viewed together.
rationales.B: Firm-level monitoring is a recommended compliance practice that complements regulatory and self-regulatory oversight rather than being displaced by it. The firm sees its own customers' order flow, account relationships, and cross-product positions at a level of detail no outside body has, which is what makes internal detection of improper coordination among customers or of wash trading feasible. Standard II(B) places the obligation on members and candidates and their firms, and deferring the task entirely to an outside body leaves it undone.
rationales.C: The practice contemplated is real-time or systematic surveillance across multiple platforms, which end-of-day exception reporting on a single venue does not satisfy on either dimension. A daily batch review cannot catch order entry and cancellation while it is happening, and a single-venue view cannot reveal potential improper coordination among customers, wash trading between related accounts, or transactions in cross-product securities that manipulate the price of an underlying security. Operational convenience is not the standard being applied.

questions.stem: Standard II(B) compliance practices most likely treat an automated order management system with pretrade controls as:

options.A: necessary for algorithmic order flow only.
options.B: discouraged, given the risk of blocking client orders.
options.C: a recommended tool for preventing manipulative orders.

rationales.A: Manipulative orders can be entered manually as readily as by an algorithm, so the controls apply to the firm's order flow generally. A trader who places and cancels orders by hand to create a false impression of supply or demand produces the same deception as a program doing it at speed, and pretrade controls screening for such patterns are equally apt. Scoping the controls to algorithmic strategies alone would leave an obvious route around them.
rationales.B: Implementation of an automated order management system and pretrade controls to identify and prevent manipulative orders is a recommended practice, not a discouraged one. Pretrade controls are calibrated to catch manipulative patterns, and the possibility that a control requires review of an occasional legitimate order is a cost the guidance accepts in exchange for stopping manipulative orders before they reach the market. The alternative, detecting the conduct only after the fact, leaves the market already misled.
rationales.C: Standard II(B) compliance practices include the implementation of an automated order management system and pretrade controls to attempt to identify and prevent manipulative orders. The point of placing the control before the order leaves the firm is that market manipulation damages market integrity at the moment the deceptive order is displayed, so prevention is worth more than detection. This sits alongside the other practices named under the standard: procedures to prevent placing and canceling orders with intent to deceive, and real-time monitoring or systematic surveillance across multiple platforms.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(B), the compliance practice recommended for a firm's trading algorithms is most likely:

options.A: an algorithmic trading ban whenever the firm holds material nonpublic information.
options.B: order-by-order manual approval before execution.
options.C: controls addressing manipulative use of trading algorithms.

rationales.A: This conflates the Standard II(B) algorithm control with a ban triggered by possession of material nonpublic information. Possession and misuse of material nonpublic information is the subject of Standard II(A), and the practice recommended under II(B) is not a blanket shutdown of algorithmic trading. What the guidance calls for is targeted controls over manipulative algorithmic activity, so algorithmic trading continues under surveillance rather than stopping.
rationales.B: Order-by-order human sign-off is not the practice described. Compliance under Standard II(B) relies on automated, systematic controls built into algorithm design, testing and monitoring, not on case-by-case approval of individual orders, which the speed and volume of algorithmic order flow would make impracticable.
rationales.C: The compliance practices listed under Standard II(B) include controls that address the use of trading algorithms for manipulative trading practices. Algorithms are a specific area of concern because their speed and complexity allow manipulative strategies such as layering, spoofing and quote stuffing to be carried out without any human reviewing the individual trades. The control therefore has to be designed into the algorithm and its monitoring, so that manipulative patterns are detected and blocked by the system itself.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(B), the compliance practice that flags individual trades deviating from expected patterns is best described as:

options.A: trade exception reporting.
options.B: pre-clearance of client orders by senior management.
options.C: periodic aggregate trading volume reporting.

rationales.A: Trade exception reporting is the compliance practice designed to identify trades that deviate from expected patterns or that trigger established thresholds, so that compliance and supervisory personnel can review those trades for possible manipulative activity. The practice works by exception: normal activity passes unexamined and only the outliers are surfaced for human judgment, which is what makes it workable in a firm that executes a large volume of orders.
rationales.B: Pre-clearance operates before execution and applies to orders without regard to whether they look unusual, so it is a different control serving a different purpose. The practice described is detective rather than authorizing, applied after the fact to the trades that depart from expected patterns or breach set thresholds, and directed at possible manipulation rather than at routine approval.
rationales.C: Aggregate volume reporting describes the firm's activity in total and cannot isolate the individual trades that matter. The practice described is aimed precisely at the single trade that departs from the expected pattern or crosses a threshold, and that trade would be invisible inside a firmwide total.

questions.stem: A multiservice firm proposes prohibiting research recommendations on the securities of its investment banking clients rather than maintaining information firewalls. This approach is best described as:

options.A: acceptable only while the offering information remains nonpublic.
options.B: preferred, and permanent for any former banking client.
options.C: impermissible, since firewalls are mandatory for such firms.

rationales.A: Prohibiting recommendations on the stock of companies that are clients of the investment banking department is a recognized alternative to firewalls, but the prohibition should not be permanent. Once an offering is complete and the material nonpublic information held by the investment banking department has become public, resuming published recommendations on that stock is not a violation of the Code and Standards, because the banking department's information no longer gives the brokerage operation any advantage in writing the report. The restriction is therefore tied to the period during which the information is still nonpublic.
rationales.B: A permanent, irrevocable prohibition goes further than the Code and Standards require and is not the best answer. It would deny research clients coverage of a company indefinitely for a conflict that expires when the information becomes public, so the restriction is temporary and tied to the engagement rather than open-ended.
rationales.C: Firewalls are the usual and best policy, but they are not the only permissible response. Prohibiting recommendations on the securities of investment banking clients is expressly recognized as an alternative, so it is wrong to say that no alternative exists or that every multiservice firm must maintain physical information barriers regardless of its size, structure or business mix.

questions.stem: Within a firm's firewall system, employee and proprietary trading is most likely:

options.A: reviewed against watch, restricted, and rumor lists.
options.B: reviewed against a single restricted list.
options.C: left unreviewed, because personal accounts are private.

rationales.A: One element of a firewall system is the review of employee trading through the maintenance of watch, restricted and rumor lists. The three lists create a layered categorization of securities under different levels of monitoring and restriction: a watch list limits knowledge of sensitive information to a few people while their trading is observed, a restricted list bars trading and sometimes research in the named securities, and a rumor list captures securities subject to market rumors that may signal an information leak.
rationales.B: The guidance describes maintaining watch, restricted and rumor lists together, not a restricted list by itself. Each list serves a distinct surveillance purpose, and a single restricted list would provide no mechanism for monitoring trading in securities that are sensitive but not yet subject to an outright trading ban.
rationales.C: Review of employee and proprietary trading through list-based monitoring is itself an element of a firewall system, so personal accounts are not beyond the firm's reach. Employees who have access to material nonpublic information accept monitoring of their trading as a condition of that access, and such review is how the firm detects misuse.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(A), firewall documentation most likely covers:

options.A: no part of the firm's information-flow regime.
options.B: the procedures and the actions taken to enforce them.
options.C: the procedures but not their enforcement.

rationales.A: Documenting both the procedures and their enforcement is an element of an effective firewall, so documenting neither is the opposite of the guidance. A firm that keeps no records also gives up its own best evidence that the barrier existed and was enforced, which is precisely what it would need to demonstrate.
rationales.B: An element of a firewall system is documentation of the procedures designed to limit the flow of information between departments and of the actions taken to enforce those procedures. Both halves matter: the written procedure shows what the barrier is meant to accomplish, and the enforcement record shows that it operated in practice. A procedure on paper with no evidence of enforcement will not establish that the firm maintained an effective barrier.
rationales.C: Documenting the procedures alone is incomplete, because the actions taken to enforce those procedures must be documented as well. Informal enforcement leaves no record that the barrier was actually applied, so the firm could not show that an employee was removed from a deal team, added to a restricted list, or denied access to information when the procedure required it.

questions.stem: While a firm is in possession of material nonpublic information, the firewall element governing its proprietary trading is most likely:

options.A: a complete halt to all proprietary trading.
options.B: normal trading supported by trader self-certification.
options.C: heightened review or restriction of that trading.

rationales.A: The element is heightened review or restriction, not an unconditional stop. Market-making and risk-arbitrage activity may properly continue while the firm holds material nonpublic information, provided it is scrutinized, because withdrawing entirely from making a market can itself signal the existence of the information and can leave clients without liquidity.
rationales.B: Self-certification by traders is not the control. The firewall element is heightened review or restriction of the activity itself, imposed and supervised by the firm, because a certification is unverifiable and cannot prevent information from reaching the desk through the ordinary course of business.
rationales.C: An element of a firewall system is heightened review or restriction of proprietary trading while the firm is in possession of material nonpublic information. Proprietary trading is a high-risk area for misuse because the firm trades for its own account and therefore captures the gain directly. Raising the level of review, or restricting the activity in the affected securities, addresses that risk while allowing legitimate functions such as market making to continue under scrutiny.

questions.stem: Regarding the handling of analyst calls, members and candidates are most likely to encourage the companies they follow to:

options.A: issue a press release before a scripted analyst call.
options.B: issue a press release before an unscripted analyst call.
options.C: hold a scripted analyst call before any press release.

rationales.A: Members and candidates should encourage companies they follow to issue press releases prior to analyst meetings and conference calls, and to script those meetings and calls to decrease the chance that further information will be disclosed. The press release puts the information in the public domain first, so nothing said on the call is material and nonpublic, and the script keeps the discussion inside what has already been released. If material nonpublic information is in fact disclosed for the first time in an analyst meeting or call, the company should be encouraged to issue a press release promptly or otherwise make the information publicly available.
rationales.B: The sequence here is right but the second half of the recommendation is missing, because scripting is recommended rather than optional. An unscripted call invites spontaneous answers that go beyond the released information, which is how material nonpublic information is selectively disclosed to the analysts on the line. Any loss of color on the call is a smaller cost than a selective disclosure, and the company remains free to release more information publicly.
rationales.C: Scripting the call does not cure the reversed sequence. The press release comes first and the meeting or call follows, so that attendees learn nothing the market does not already have. Holding the call first in order to reward attentive analysts is the selective disclosure the practice is designed to prevent.

questions.stem: Under the mosaic theory, an analyst who assembles a recommendation from public and nonmaterial nonpublic information is most likely advised to:

options.A: save and document all of the underlying research.
options.B: purge the underlying research files periodically.
options.C: retain the final research report alone.

rationales.A: Analysts are free to use mosaic information in their research reports, but they should save and document all of their research. Evidence of the analyst's knowledge of public and nonmaterial nonpublic information about a corporation strengthens the assertion that the conclusions were reached solely through appropriate methods rather than through the use of material nonpublic information. The documentation is the analyst's defense: it shows the chain of inference from permissible inputs to the conclusion.
rationales.B: Purging the files destroys the record that supports the analyst's position. Without the underlying research there is nothing to show that the conclusion came from assembling public and nonmaterial pieces, which leaves the analyst exposed to the inference that a material nonpublic source explained the call.
rationales.C: The final report alone does not demonstrate how the conclusion was reached. The underlying notes and sources are exactly what show that the mosaic was built from public and nonmaterial nonpublic information, so discarding them removes the evidence that matters most.

questions.stem: Under Standard II(B), an analyst publishing earnings projections is most likely to:

options.A: publish a single point estimate as an unambiguous forecast.
options.B: publish a range of outcomes with the assumptions disclosed.
options.C: publish conclusions while withholding the model assumptions.

rationales.A: An unambiguous single figure looks more useful to clients, but a bare point estimate is what invites the manipulation concern. Presented without a range or the assumptions behind it, an aggressive single figure can be used to pressure a company into revising its guidance, and that is information-based manipulation rather than analysis. Framing the projection as a range of possible outcomes is the acceptable practice.
rationales.B: The acceptable practice is to write a report that frames the earnings projection in a range of possible outcomes and clearly outlines the assumptions used in the models, including the relevant findings from the analyst's own research. The range conveys the genuine uncertainty in the forecast, and the disclosed assumptions let readers judge the analysis for themselves and reproduce it. Together they distinguish legitimate research, however aggressive its conclusion, from an exaggerated projection published to move a company or its share price.
rationales.C: Clearly outlining the assumptions used in the models is the second half of the acceptable practice, so treating them as proprietary defeats it. A conclusion that cannot be examined gives readers no way to assess whether the forecast is supported, which is the condition under which an extreme projection becomes manipulative.

questions.stem: Nonpublic deal information held by a multiservice firm's investment banking department reaches its sales staff in the ordinary course of business. The firm's most appropriate action would have been to:

options.A: require the sales staff to sign confidentiality agreements.
options.B: rely on the discretion of the individual employees.
options.C: adopt information barriers between its departments.

rationales.A: Confidentiality agreements bind the people who already have the information; they do not stop it from reaching them. The failure here is structural, in that nonpublic deal information crossed out of the department that held it into one with no need for it, and a signature does not cure the exposure that created.
rationales.B: The lesson is firm-level rather than individual. A firm cannot rely on each employee's judgment to contain material nonpublic information that ordinary interdepartmental contact puts in front of them; the firm must establish the barrier, since personnel will otherwise encounter such information in the normal course of business.
rationales.C: The firm should have adopted information barriers to prevent the communication of nonpublic information between its departments. Firewalls, meaning physical and informational separation of the investment banking function from sales and research, are the best policy for preventing a violation of Standard II(A). They address exactly this exposure: separate space, restricted systems access and controlled communication keep deal information inside the department that holds it, so that personnel elsewhere in the firm do not encounter it in the normal course of business.

questions.stem: An employee behind a firewall who believes he or she needs to share confidential information with someone on the other side is most likely required to:

options.A: never share the information.
options.B: consult the designated compliance officer.
options.C: arrange the sharing with that colleague.

rationales.A: Standard II(A) contemplates controlled wall-crossing rather than an absolute bar on sharing. Information may cross the firewall when the sharing is necessary, provided a designated compliance officer determines that it is necessary, decides how much may be shared, and coordinates the process. A rule that no information may ever cross would make the designated-officer procedure pointless.
rationales.B: Under Standard II(A), an employee behind a firewall who believes that he or she needs to share confidential information with someone on the other side of the firewall should consult a designated compliance officer to determine whether sharing the information is necessary and how much information should be shared. If the sharing is necessary, the compliance officer should coordinate the process of 'looking over the wall' so that the necessary information will be shared and the integrity of the procedure will be maintained. The compliance officer is the control point for both decisions: whether to share at all, and how much.
rationales.C: Sharing across the wall must be coordinated through the designated compliance officer, not arranged bilaterally. The officer judges whether the sharing is necessary, limits how much is disclosed, and supervises the look over the wall. A private arrangement between the two employees bypasses that review and defeats the integrity of the firewall procedure.

questions.stem: Employer practices restricting employees' personal trading most likely include:

options.A: a prohibition on firm monitoring of employees' personal accounts.
options.B: monitoring, periodic reports, and restricted and watch lists.
options.C: an annual ethics attestation.

rationales.A: Firm monitoring of personal trading is itself one of the recognized employer practices for preventing misuse of material nonpublic information, so a program that bars monitoring omits a central control. Employees' personal accounts are precisely where misuse of confidential information surfaces, which is why monitoring sits alongside reporting and list maintenance rather than being displaced by them.
rationales.B: Such practices may include firm monitoring of personal trading, mandating periodic reports of personal transactions, and implementing a restricted list and watch list of companies, which Standard II(A) sets out among the compliance practices for complying with personal trading limitations. The combination of monitoring, reporting, and list maintenance forms a comprehensive personal trading compliance program: monitoring detects trading in sensitive names, periodic reports give the firm a record against which that monitoring can be tested, and the restricted and watch lists tell employees in advance which securities are off limits or under heightened scrutiny.
rationales.C: An annual attestation is a statement by the employee, not a control over the employee's trading. The practices contemplated are continuous: firm monitoring of personal trading, mandated periodic reports of personal transactions, and a restricted list and watch list of companies.
